newsitem.title: FRANCE: Council of Europe votes to admit Croatia - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Council of Europe votes to admit Croatia - diplomats.

text.p: The Council of Europe decided on Wednesday to admit Croatia as its 40th member next month after a six-month delay over human rights concerns, diplomats said.
Croatia will officially become a member of the organisation, which promotes democracy and human rights, on November 6, they added.

Regarded as an antechamber to the European Union, the Strasbourg-based Council froze Zagreb's application in May and set conditions concerning respect of the Dayton peace agreement on former Yugoslavia, democracy and press freedom.

Wednesday's decision, taken by representatives of the body's Council of Ministers, reflects a majority view that Croatia had made sufficient progress to justify admission to the pan-European organisation, diplomats said.

Croatian Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa had on Tuesday expressed confidence that Croatia would be accepted into the Council of Europe, following talks with European Commisssioner Hans van den Broek and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana.
Commission sources said van den Broek had told Matesa he hoped EU member states would take a positive decision on admitting Croatia in early November, provided the conditions have been met.
Diplomats said Germany, Croatia's main ally in the EU, had pressed strongly for Zagreb to be "rewarded for good behaviour".
In July, the Council formally invited Croatia to join but said entry would be delayed until it was satisfied President Franjo Tudjman had complied fully with the Dayton accord.
Since then, elections have been held successfully in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and rump Yugoslavia have established diplomatic relations.
Progress has also been made on an amnesty law for Serbs who rebelled against Zagreb in 1991, the diplomats said.

On democracy and human rights, journalists charged with libelling the government have been acquitted and the country has adopted a new press law, although there are still concerns about minority rights and the Zagreb city council, they said.
